feedback: D1: You built a clean ten-row catalogue with OWASP class and CWE for each item, and you correctly identified the safe Base64URL helper as the decoy while refusing to mislabel alg:none as the decoy, which trips up many. Your CWE choices are defensible even where they differ from the key, MD5 as CWE-328 and the hardcoded secret as CWE-321 both stand. The real gap is that you missed the stored XSS in comments entirely (the 02:18:47 capture beacons a cookie to 185.220.101.9:8443, OWASP A03 / CWE-79), and you substituted error-message disclosure (CWE-209) in its place, so the ten are not the ten. The catalogue also describes evidence more than it quotes it, the strong verbatim lines only appear over in D3. Your decoy verdict is right but thin, you assert b64url only decodes without proving the mechanism, name that the HS256 branch uses hash_equals() which is constant-time, that is what makes it sound. D2: Your chain runs in the right order from SQLi through admin, JWT forgery, XXE, file read, to the 312-row exfil, and crediting the exfil hop with S:C for the scope change to the shared internal service is the senior insight we wanted. But every hop says timestamp Not provided, you never reconciled a single hop to a capture line (recon 02:14:08, SQLi 02:15:31, file read 02:24:02), and you dropped the recon, failed-guess, stored-XSS and open-redirect hops. Your SQLi CVSS uses A:H, it should be A:N, the auth bypass does not affect availability, so the score is nearer 9.1 than 9.8. You stated the assumption honestly that the pack lacks cost figures, which I credit, but you gave no naira estimate at all, the balances up to ~950k NGN summing to tens of millions across 312 customers six weeks before BoltCash was reachable. D3: This is your strongest piece. The exec summary is jargon-free, the threat model is real, findings are tied to quoted source and capture line numbers, the decoy verdict is correctly stated, and crucially you ordered remediation by risk reduction and effort and said so explicitly, not by CVSS, which earns the big row. Two things hold it back, the exec summary ends on 312 customers but never lands a naira headline, and your two detection stopgaps name the right field (username, XML body) but give a qualitative false-positive level (Low, Very Low) rather than an actual rate. D4: You answer the four prompts in your own voice and anchor to the 312 records, good. But the ISC2 canons are cited only generically as 1/2/3 without being load-bearing to a specific dilemma, and your NDPA reference names the duty without the sections, cite section 40 (notify NDPC within 72 hours) and section 41 (notify the 312 data subjects on high risk) by number. I looked hard for a way to push this into the 70s and the evidence did not support it, the missing stored-XSS finding, the absent timestamp reconciliation in D2, and the wrong SQLi availability metric are real point losses, not roundable. The single most important fix: reconcile every exploit hop to its exact capture timestamp and quote the line, that one habit lifts both D1 and D2 at once.
